#### About Ralph Waldo Emerson

Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was the American Transcendentalist essayist and lecturer who urged self-reliance and unbroken relation to nature and the Over-Soul. A former Unitarian minister in Concord, he gathered the Dial circle and mentored younger writers including Thoreau.

### Interpretation

Emerson is not praising inconsistency; he is attacking a particular motive for consistency. His target is the person who refuses to change because they fear appearing to have been wrong, which he calls a hobgoblin — a small fear governing a mind. The claim is that this motive is external, so the resulting consistency is a form of deference. What he wants instead is coherence of a different kind, supplied by present conviction rather than by past statements.

#### Why it matters

It separates two reasons for standing by something: that it is right, or that you once said it. Only the first is a reason.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little…”?

“A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little…” comes from Self-Reliance (1841 (in Essays: First Series)), attributed to Ralph Waldo Emerson.

#### What does Ralph Waldo Emerson mean by courage?

Philosophers ask whether courage is fearlessness or right action amid fear, and how it relates to recklessness, endurance, and moral courage in public life. This passage enters that discussion through courage.
